scenario: AITA for playing music in the middle of the day when my roommate has a weird sleep schedule? | So I live in a 3 bedroom duplex with 2 other girls. The duplex is laid out with two bedrooms up stairs with a bathroom in the middle. Downstairs is the living room, kitchen, dining room and roomates room and her own bathroom. When we picked rooms I picked first because I moved in first and then my roommate upstairs picked and then the girl downstairs. She wasn’t too happy with her room because it was the smallest and the location but settled because she had her own bathroom. So the roommate downstairs has a very weird schedule. Sometimes she works nights and sometimes mornings. Sometimes she has 5 hour days and other days she can work 13. So obviously with the constant changing work schedule her sleeping schedule has became very weird and erratic and we never know when she’s asleep now. So since I can never guess when she’s asleep I often so downstairs in the kitchen and make food and play music on my speaker while I meal prep. It’s apart of my routine through out the day that i really enjoy since I don’t work till 2pm. But yesterday my roommate downstairs texted our group chat and asked us to please stop playing music in the kitchen at any time of the day. She said it wakes her up almost every time and when she is a wake it’s just very disruptive. My other roommate said sure but I said that’s not really fair because she often plays music too in the kitchen. She told me it wasn’t really fair that she had the shittiest room in the house and that if I wanted to switch with her so she wouldn’t have to be woken up by it that would be fine. Of course I said no and said I was going to keep playing music because it’s noon usually when I do it and it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule. Both my roommates are saying I’m being an asshole and that it’s the least I can do because I have the best room in the house because it’s the most separate. I honestly think they are being assholes because why should I have to be so quiet I’m the middle of the day!?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0** (not AITA, but there’s room for compromise and better communication). Here’s why: ### **Key Issues in This Scenario:** 1. **Noise Sensitivity vs. Personal Routine** - Your roommate’s sleep schedule is erratic, and music at any time can disrupt her rest. While your routine is important to you, her well-being (especially given her unpredictable work hours) should also be considered. - Playing music in the kitchen is likely audible to her room (especially if it’s a small space), making it harder to ignore. 2. **Fairness vs. Fairness** - Your argument that "she plays music too" is valid, but context matters. If she’s playing music at times that don’t conflict with others’ schedules (e.g., during her own work hours), it’s less disruptive. Your music is consistently during daytime hours when others are likely resting or working. - Your room is "better" in terms of separation, but that doesn’t mean you should have unlimited freedom to disrupt others. Shared spaces (like the kitchen) are for everyone’s use, and noise levels should be considerate. 3. **Communication Breakdown** - You dismissed her request outright ("it’s noon, it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule"). This comes across as dismissive, even if you believe your routine is reasonable. - Offering to switch rooms isn’t a fair solution—her room isn’t the issue; her sleep needs are. Instead, you could propose: - Lowering volume or avoiding music during her known rest periods (even if unpredictable). - Using headphones or a speaker in a different location (e.g., your room). - Setting a general "quiet hours" guideline for shared spaces (e.g., no loud music between 10 AM–4 PM). 4. **Roommate Dynamics** - Both roommates calling you an asshole suggests your tone and refusal to compromise are escalating tension. Roommates often have to make small sacrifices for harmony, especially in shared living spaces. ### **Why It’s Not Just "Fair" to Keep Playing Music:** - **Shared responsibility**: You’re not the only one who benefits from the kitchen. Her discomfort is a valid concern, especially since she’s already dealing with an irregular schedule. - **Power dynamics**: You moved in first and picked your room, which gives you a slight advantage in negotiation. Using that to justify louder behavior isn’t sustainable. - **Long-term living**: If this continues, resentment will build. Roommates who feel their needs are ignored often leave or create hostile environments. ### **What You Could Do Instead:** 1. **Acknowledge her concern** (even if you disagree): *"I hear you, and I’ll try to keep the volume lower or avoid music during her rest times. Can we figure out a schedule that works for everyone?"* 2. **Propose a compromise**: - *"I’ll use headphones or move the speaker to my room when I’m cooking."* - *"If she texts when she’s sleeping, I’ll pause the music."* 3. **Address the root issue**: - Suggest the group chat discuss general kitchen noise rules (e.g., no loud music after 10 AM). - If her sleep schedule is chronically disrupted, encourage her to look into solutions (e.g., blackout curtains, white noise machines). ### **Final Thought:** You’re not *wrong* for enjoying music, but dismissing her request without effort to accommodate her needs is unreasonable. Roommate conflicts often come down to balance—your routine matters, but so does hers. A little flexibility goes a long way in maintaining a peaceful living situation. Would you like help drafting a message to your roommates to de-escalate?
